summary: Defines version 2 of the Service Location Protocol, a framework that lets computers discover network services such as printers with little or no manual configuration. It is designed to scale from small networks to larger ones.

eli5.summary: Walk into a mall and ask a directory screen where the shoe shop is. Computers use this to ask the network where a printer or other helper is.

questions: how do hosts discover printers automatically
what is a directory agent in slp
subtitle: How computers find printers, servers and other network services without being told where they are.

tldr.problem: Users and programs normally need to know a service's host name before they can use it, which means a lot of manual configuration.
tldr.mechanism: User Agents ask for a service type and attributes by multicast, or by unicast to a Directory Agent that caches what Service Agents have registered, and get back the service's URL. Scopes group services, and optional signed authentication blocks protect the data.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates SLPv1 (RFC 2165) and was itself updated by RFC 3224. It is meant for networks under cooperative administration, not the whole Internet.

today: RFC 2608 is a Proposed Standard published in June 1999. It updates SLPv1 (RFC 2165) and has itself been updated by RFC 3224. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Applicability
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol (SLP) gives hosts information about the existence, location and configuration of networked services. Instead of knowing a host name, the user supplies a type of service and a set of attributes describing it, and SLP resolves the network address.

This document updates SLPv1 (RFC 2165), correcting protocol errors, adding some enhancements and removing some requirements. It has two parts: the required features, then optional extended features that allow greater scalability.

The applicability statement is blunt. SLP is intended for networks under cooperative administrative control. It was designed for enterprise networks with shared services and may not scale to wide-area discovery across the global Internet, or to networks with hundreds of thousands of clients or tens of thousands of services.
sections.eli5: Normally you must know the name of the computer that has the printer. This lets you just ask for 'a printer' and be told where one is.

sections.title: Agents and Protocol Overview
sections.content:
SLP has three kinds of agent. A User Agent (UA) works for the user and looks for services. A Service Agent (SA) advertises one or more services. A Directory Agent (DA) collects advertisements and gives the protocol its scalability.

Without a DA, the UA multicasts a Service Request (SrvRqst) and any SA that offers a matching service unicasts back a Service Reply (SrvRply) with its location. In larger networks a DA acts as a cache. SAs send SrvReg messages to register and receive SrvAck in reply, and these registrations expire unless refreshed. UAs then send their requests by unicast to the DA.

UAs and SAs find DAs in two ways: they multicast a request for the service type service:directory-agent at start-up, and they listen for the DA's infrequent unsolicited advertisements (DAAdvert). DA locations can also be statically configured or learned through DHCP.

An SLPv2 implementation SHOULD support SLPv1. SLPv1 and SLPv2 agents cannot hear each other directly, so they interoperate only if an SLPv2 DA that supports both versions is present.
sections.eli5: If nobody keeps a list, you shout your question and whoever can help answers. In a big place, a helper keeps a notebook of who offers what, and you just ask the helper.

sections.title: Service URLs and Attributes
sections.content:
A service's location is given as a URL. It can use the service: scheme, for example service:tftp://myhost, or any other URL scheme, in which case the service type is the scheme name (http for an http URL). An abstract type has the form service:abstract-type:concrete-type, and a request for service:printer matches both service:printer:lpr://hostname and service:printer:http://hostname.

A Naming Authority can follow a dot in the type. It defines the meaning of service types and attributes, and IANA is implied when none is given.

Services are described by attributes, written as an attribute list such as (name=value),keyword. Values can be integers, strings, booleans or opaque byte sequences. Reserved characters must be escaped as a backslash plus two hexadecimal digits, and non-standard attribute names SHOULD begin with x-. Requests can carry an LDAPv3 search filter as a predicate, for example (&(q<=3)(speed>=1000)).
sections.eli5: A service is described like a shop sign: the kind of shop, plus details such as the opening hours. You can ask for any shop that matches the details you care about.

sections.title: Message Header and Message Types
sections.content:
All SLP messages start with a header holding the version, a Function-ID, the message length, flags, a Next Extension Offset, an XID and a Language Tag. All length fields are in network byte order, and strings are UTF-8, not null terminated, and preceded by a two byte length.

The flags are OVERFLOW (0x80), set when a message is too big for a datagram, FRESH (0x40), set on every new registration, and REQUEST MCAST (0x20), set when a request is multicast or broadcast. The XID identifies a request, and a retransmission uses the same XID. Replies copy it, and only unsolicited DAAdverts use an XID of 0.

UAs and SAs MUST support SrvRqst, SrvRply and DAAdvert, and SAs MUST also support SrvReg, SAAdvert and SrvAck. The other messages are optional for them but mandatory for DAs. They let a UA browse service types (SrvTypeRqst), ask for attributes (AttrRqst) and let an SA withdraw a service (SrvDeReg).

Errors are returned only for unicast requests. A multicast request that would cause an error is silently discarded.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a label saying what kind of message it is, how long it is and which question it answers, so replies can be matched with questions.

sections.title: Transport, Registration and Retransmission
sections.content:
SLP uses UDP port 427. Requests are multicast to the administratively scoped address 239.255.255.253 with a default TTL of 255, and broadcast can be used on isolated networks. The default maximum size of a UDP message is 1400 bytes. If a reply does not fit, it is truncated with the OVERFLOW flag set, and the UA MAY retry over TCP. A SrvReg or SrvDeReg too large for a datagram MUST be sent over TCP.

An SA registers each service with a DA, giving a URL, a lifetime, a service type, scopes and an attribute list. The lifetime can be any value between 0 and 0xffff (around 18 hours), and the SA SHOULD re-register before it expires. A registration with FRESH set replaces any previous registration entirely. Without FRESH it is an incremental update: for example, a service registered with A=1, B=2, C=3 and then updated with C=30, D=40 ends up with A=1, B=2, C=30, D=40. Incremental updates MUST NOT be used for services registered with authentication blocks.

Requests that get no response are retransmitted with exponentially increasing waits, doubling each time. Multicast requests carry a Previous Responder List (PRList) so agents that already answered stay silent, and the UA stops when no new answers arrive or the list would no longer fit in a datagram.
sections.eli5: If nobody answers your shout, you wait a bit and try again, waiting longer each time. People who already answered are listed so they do not answer twice.

sections.title: Scopes and Directory Agents
sections.content:
A scope is a set of services, usually an administrative group. The default scope string is DEFAULT, and scope strings are case insensitive. A message that lacks a scope the receiver is configured for is dropped if multicast, or answered with SCOPE_NOT_SUPPORTED if unicast.

Scopes are the primary way an administrator scales SLP. With administrative scoping, UAs and SAs are configured with scope lists (possibly by DHCP options 78 and 79) so users only see the services meant for them. With user selectable scopes, a UA is given no scope and learns them from DAAdverts or SAAdverts, leaving the choice to the user.

DAs cache service information to improve performance and scalability, and several DAs can store the same registrations for robustness. Each DA multicasts an unsolicited DAAdvert every CONFIG_DA_BEAT seconds and includes a boot timestamp, so SAs can tell whether it lost its registrations and need to re-register. A timestamp of 0 means the DA is going down.
sections.eli5: Scopes are like school classes. You only see the notices posted for your class, unless you are allowed to look at all of them.

sections.title: Authentication Blocks
sections.content:
Optional authentication blocks let an agent check that URLs, attribute lists and advertisements were not modified and came from an authorized agent. Each block holds a Block Structure Descriptor, a length, a timestamp saying when the signature expires, an SLP SPI string and the signature data. The SLP SPI names the keying material and parameters needed to verify it.

All SLP agents MUST implement DSA with SHA-1 (BSD 0x0002). SAs MUST register services with DSA authentication blocks when they are configured to sign, and DAs MUST use them in unsolicited DAAdverts. A DA keeps registrations protected: a later re-registration or deregistration must carry a block for each SPI used originally, or the DA returns an AUTHENTICATION_ABSENT error.
sections.eli5: A signature on a note proves who wrote it and that nobody changed it. The reader needs to know your signature in advance to check it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SLP can authenticate service URLs and attributes, but only systems that administrators configured in advance can generate signatures. SLP provides no confidentiality. Sites that need it should use the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).

If agents neither generate nor verify authentication blocks, an adversary could advertise services on servers it controls and gain access to users' private information, or carry out selective denial of service attacks. Sites in hostile environments, for example those directly connected to the Internet, should consider distributing keys before deploying sensitive agents.

The RFC also notes that SLP is useful as a bootstrap protocol with no preconfiguration. In that case the security mechanisms cannot be used and a certain amount of 'blind faith' is required.
sections.eli5: If nobody checks signatures, a trickster can put up a fake sign pointing to their own shop. Signing and checking stops that, but it needs set-up first.
